passages.t: Asa buys help from Aram, and Hanani's rebuke
passages.happening:
‘In the thirty-sixth year of Asa’s reign, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and fortified Ramah’ (verse 1), to cut Judah off. Asa takes the silver and gold from the treasuries of the temple and the palace and sends them to Ben-hadad king of Aram in Damascus, asking him to break his treaty with Baasha (verses 2-3). Ben-hadad attacks Israel's northern towns, Baasha stops building, and Asa uses Baasha's stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah (verses 4-6).

Then Hanani the seer comes to Asa: “Because you have relied on the king of Aram and not on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Aram has escaped from your hand” (verse 7). He reminds him of the Cushites and Libyans, defeated when Asa relied on God (verse 8). ‘For the eyes of the LORD roam to and fro over all the earth, to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him’ (verse 9). ‘Asa was angry with the seer and became so enraged over this matter that he put the man in prison. And at the same time Asa oppressed some of the people’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 14 and 15 showed a king who sought God and relied on him. This is the sad second half. The same verb that described Asa's faith, rely, sha'an, now describes his trust in a foreign king; it comes three times in Hanani's rebuke. The Chronicler presents Asa as a warning that a good beginning does not promise a faithful end.

First Kings 15 records the conflict with Baasha and the deal with Ben-hadad; Chronicles adds Hanani's rebuke and Asa's harsh answer. Ramah lay a few miles north of Jerusalem on the main road, so fortifying it would have choked Judah's way north. Ben-hadad's attack fell on towns near the sources of the Jordan. Buying a larger power's help against a neighbor was a common strategy, and Israel's prophets repeatedly condemned it as trusting human power instead of God.

The dates raise a puzzle. Kings has Baasha die in Asa's twenty-sixth year, so he could not campaign in Asa's thirty-sixth. Some count the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth years from the division of the kingdom rather than from Asa's accession, which would put the war around his sixteenth year. Others suggest a copying error in the numbers.

Verse 9 states the principle of the whole book in one sentence. The verb roam, shut, pictures God's eyes ranging over the earth, not to catch people out but to find those he can strengthen. Folly, sakal, in the Old Testament is a failure to live in the light of God, not low intelligence.
passages.later: Isaiah said, ‘Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who rely on horses’ (Isaiah 31:1), and ‘They do not look to the Holy One of Israel; they do not seek the LORD’ (Isaiah 31:1).
passages.asks: Asa had once relied on God against a vast army, and later paid for help with the temple's silver. Ask what you reach for first when you are hemmed in. And ask how you respond when someone tells you the truth about it, with anger or with listening.

passages.happening: ‘In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa became diseased in his feet, and his malady became increasingly severe. Yet even in his illness he did not seek the LORD, but only the physicians’ (verse 12). Asa dies in the forty-first year of his reign (verse 13). He is buried in the tomb he had cut for himself in the City of David, laid on a bier full of spices and blended perfumes, ‘then they made a great fire in his honor’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Asa's reign began with a command to seek the LORD and ends with a king who seeks only human help. The irony is in the words. Physicians are literally healers, from rapha, the verb God uses of himself when he says he is Israel's healer.

Seeking physicians was not itself wrong. The Old Testament describes remedies, and the complaint here is that Asa sought only physicians and not the LORD. Some think his physicians used foreign or magical practices, but the text does not say so, and it is better not to build on the guess. The great fire at his burial was not cremation; it was a ceremonial burning of spices in the king's honor, also mentioned in Jeremiah and withheld from the disgraced king Jehoram.

Kings says only that in his old age he became diseased in his feet. The Chronicler does not say that the illness was a punishment, and these notes do not either.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.later: Isaiah told Hezekiah's attendants, “Prepare a poultice of figs” (2 Kings 20:7), and Hezekiah recovered. Paul sends greetings from ‘Luke, the beloved physician’ (Colossians 4:14).
passages.hard:
Is it wrong for a believer to go to a doctor?

The chapter does not condemn medicine. Its complaint is that Asa sought only the physicians and did not seek the LORD, which fits the whole chapter: he relied on human resources in place of God. Elsewhere Scripture treats remedies with approval, as when Isaiah prescribes a poultice of figs for Hezekiah, and the New Testament includes Luke, whom Paul calls the beloved physician. Christian teaching has generally held that seeking medical care and seeking God belong together, and that the danger lies in trusting any human help as though God were not needed.
passages.asks: Asa sought the physicians and not the LORD, when he could have sought both. Ask whether you bring your body's troubles to God as well as to those who treat them. And ask who around you is ill and needs you to pray with them, not to explain their illness.
